text:
A 13-year-old student has developed a system that significantly reduced carbon dioxide in seawater during experiments, offering a promising approach to protecting coral reefs and shellfish in coastal countries like the Philippines.

Raji Doshi, an eighth-grader from Connecticut, United States, created ALKACORE by combining seaweed with a natural mineral. Her invention won the 2026 3M Young Scientist Challenge, earning her $25,000 and the title of America's Top Young Scientist, organizers announced October 14.

Her project tackles ocean acidification. As seawater absorbs carbon dioxide, it becomes more acidic, making it harder for corals, oysters and other marine animals to build and maintain their shells and protective structures.

The problem is especially relevant to the Philippines, where coral reefs and marine resources sustain fishing communities and coastal livelihoods. The Department of Science and Technology has studied seawater conditions at 63 locations nationwide to help identify areas vulnerable to ocean acidification.

ALKACORE uses seaweed to absorb carbon dioxide as it grows. A naturally occurring mineral called aragonite helps reduce acidity in the water. According to 3M, Raji's experiments showed that adding aragonite increased seaweed growth and substantially lowered dissolved carbon dioxide.

She also developed a computer model to calculate how much mineral the system needs, helping refine its potential use in coastal areas.

Her idea began with a love of collecting seashells. After learning how ocean acidity threatens the animals that create them, Raji decided to investigate a solution.

“Raji's project reminds us that when you're passionate about something, you can use that interest to change the world,” said Deborah Isabelle, a 3M specialist who mentored her.

Raji defeated nine other finalists aged 11 to 14 during the October 12 and 13 competition in Minnesota. Her research offers a direction for future efforts to protect marine ecosystems, including the coastal waters on which many Filipino communities depend.

Honestly, I don’t think you’re asking in good faith because none of your arguments have been made in good faith, either that or you’re spectacularly ignorant of 20th century history. But I’ll humor you because someone else may read it. 

Everyday life under Cuban socialism has meant chronic scarcity and regimentation since the early 1960s. By the mid-1960s the ration book controlled nearly everything an ordinary family could obtain. A typical monthly allotment offered about six pounds of rice, a pound and a half of beans, two pounds of cooking fat, a few eggs, and only occasional scraps of meat or chicken. I remember in Cuba frog legs became a thing because there was no chicken in the supermarket.  And no, Cubans are not fond of French frog cuisine. 

People stood in long lines for hours, often to discover the item had already run out. Clothing was equally restricted: one pair of pants or a dress and a single pair of shoes per year, all of similar cut and fabric. Students were sent for weeks of compulsory farm labor in crude camps with bad food. When you reached of the age of 12, you were taken out of your parents home and sent by yourself to a farm school on the other side of the island, were you spent the morning in class, and the afternoons doing slave labor in the fields 

Neighborhood committees (Comités de Defensa de la Revolución) watched neighbors and reported deviations from Marxist orthodoxy, leading to detention, arrest, and imprisonment. The result was monotony, hunger, and constant calculation over the next meal.

Sixty years later the pattern remains. Average state wages buy roughly nine dollars a month on the informal market. Frequent blackouts lasting many hours leave refrigerators useless and apartments dark. Families skip meals because rice, oil, and eggs cost more than their income allows. Water arrives irregularly. Medicine and fuel are scarce. People spend large parts of each day searching for the basics the state still fails to provide. 

Emigration— legal and illegal— is the main exit for those who can leave. The everyday experience is one of persistent material shortage under a system that has never delivered reliable abundance or ordinary choice.

Here’s something you have never seen; an American making a rickety homemade raft and launching themselves into some of the most dangerous waters on Earth, to escape the United States and go to Cuba.

text:
CONSERVATIVE FRIENDS: PLEASE READ BEFORE VOTING ON AMENDMENT B.
tl;dr: this is a battle for control over of your property taxes, and the ability to continue socializing them for donors, and I believe powerful interests are getting in front of any effort to reform this broken system as was necessary in 20 other states who had similar issues before and where voters finally took action. I do not believe a good faith reading has anything to do with protecting you from outside groups wanting to raise taxes (the record below shows that). I believe lobbyists for developers and their preferred legislators are the progenitors of this initiative and behind this campaign. Please vote NO, so we can right the wrongs the legislature has given us vis-à-vis socialized costs and private profits for their donors, and as is demonstrated below any property tax restructuring will almost certainly require a 60% vote per this Amendment. They know the political winds are turning hard on property taxes and this bill is designed to frustrate any citizen led effort on the topic. All the receipts are below, please read and share this post as time is short to beat back this bad faith Amendment.
----------
The claims:
With that out of the way, let’s evaluate the claims as being presented by the legislature and its big money backers to voters.

The first and most obvious is that, despite your lying eyes of being in the highest taxed red state, they’re desperate to protect you from higher taxes. And that groups like MWEG have ulterior motives to further increase the highest tax burden of any red state, and the threat was so severe that it necessitates a constitutional amendment in 2026. Let’s evaluate the evidence to assess how real this threat is in 2026:

· “Out-of-state special interest money”(Rep. Blake Moore, Hesterman, AFP). Amendment B limits votes, not money. Utah has no contribution limits at all, and the legislature refuses to change this. And the YES side’s own organizations on Ballotpedia’s list are Americans for Prosperity–Utah and Americans for Tax Reform, both national groups
· “You can’t vote out your neighbors.” You don’t need to; the Legislature rewrote all three 2018 initiatives by simple majority (Prop 2 in December 2018, Prop 3 in February 2019, Prop 4 in 2020). Voters have no such recourse against the Legislature’s tax votes.
· “It protects taxpayers.” From voters, and in name only. The Legislature raises taxes on a simple majority with no public vote, and in 2018 it froze the school property tax levy, about $125 million a year in increases nobody voted on. Rep. Dailey-Provost’s offer to apply 60% to legislators went nowhere.

And countervailing all this is the hysteria by its proponents about boogeyman left wing groups is that any tax increase, can be undone by a simple legislative majority, period. So, all this nonsense about your legislators being the only officials you can trust is not credible, and I’d characterize it in some cases as bad faith gaslighting in some cases, but in most cases it’s good people that have been co-opted by a deceptive narrative being spun by those with undisclosed agendas at work.

And before someone addresses it in the comments, I want to point out that the 2024 Supreme Court ruling on initiatives does not at all cover taxation, so constitutionally, any tax some left-wing group pushed (as the sponsors tell us we need to protect against), could be repealed by a simple majority in the legislature.

So if there exists no known initiative this is meant to counter (per the Sponsors’ own admissions), and also in reality does not even preclude the legislature from undoing a bad initiative voters were duped into voting for, then what exactly is going on here with this massive push with money from out-of-state lobbyists such as the AFP-Utah to desperately get us to take away our ability to influence our taxation?

Hint, it has everything to do with the continued socialization of your property taxes for the benefit of developers.

But before getting into the practical consequences of how devastating this 60% threshold will be against a potential reform movement, let’s talk about the track record of those in the legislature trying to protect us against these invisible tax boogeyman over the past 5 years. Nearly every single time a bill came up to curb the ability to raise taxes, give us a bill of rights, or otherwise protect us from developers who’ve figured out how to prime us for their private profits, the legislature has rejected it, and here are the receipts:

2022
HB478, Rep. Brad Last (R). Ended the school basic-levy freeze a year early and repealed the WPU value rate. Passed the House 56-13, died in Senate Rules.
HB128, Rep. Mike Kohler (R). Repealed the 1995 school impact fee ban so districts could charge impact fees. Never assigned to a committee.

2023
HB260, Rep. Joel Briscoe (D). Raised the circuit breaker income cap to $50,000. Passed the House 68-0, pulled into Senate Rules; the Senate tax chair said he preferred deferral.
HB454, Rep. Kera Birkeland (R). Senior cap: taxes could rise no more than 5% a year for homeowners 70+ under $50,000 income. Listed in committee, never considered.
HB296, Rep. Walt Brooks (R) and SB 141, Sen. Wayne Harper (R). Cut the statewide school levy by $100M–$128M. Neither was ever assigned to a      committee.
SJR1, Sen. Dan McCay (R). Would have let the Legislature exempt more than 45% of home value. The committee stripped that language after Utah      Taxpayers Association opposition; the remainder died in House Rules.
HB298, Rep. Candice Pierucci (R). Full primary-residence exemption for 100%-disabled veterans. Died in House Rules.
HB372, Rep. James Cobb (R). Let voters refer school-board tax increases to the ballot. On the agenda, never discussed.

2024
HB354, Rep. Tyler Clancy (R). Voter approval before any entity exceeds its certified rate through 2026. Never heard.
HB173, Rep. Candice Pierucci (R). School-board tax referendum. Passed the House 42-28; the Senate committee listed it and skipped it.
HB512, Rep. Walt Brooks (R). Cut the school levy by $75M. Never assigned to a committee.
SB146, Sen. Keith Grover (R). Senior and disabled “work-off” credit against property tax. Never heard.

2025
SB224, Sen. Wayne Harper (R). Raised the circuit breaker limit to $46,000 and the top credit to $2,000. Never assigned to a committee.
HJR7 and HB428, Rep. Jill Koford (R). Raise the primary residential exemption to 50%, with constitutional room to 55%. HJR 7 never left Rules;      the 50% was stripped from HB 428 before passage.
HB511, Rep. Tiara Auxier (R). Voter opinion question before revenue increases, plus a cap on retained new-growth revenue. Held in committee      9-0.
HB 408, Rep. Rex Shipp (R). School-board referendum including tax increases. Passed the House 40-33, failed in Senate committee 3-4.

2026
SB97, Sen. Dan McCay (R). As filed, a 5% cap on Truth-in-Taxation increases; rewritten into fund-balance limits and a one-exemption-per-household rule. Died on the Senate floor 14-15.
HJR 7 and HB 161, Rep. Jill Koford (R). Primary residential exemption to 60%. Assigned to committee, never heard; Koford cited business opposition.
HB 484, Rep. Kay Christofferson (R). 5% cap on Truth-in-Taxation revenue growth unless voters approve more. Held in committee 7-3 after two hours of testimony.
HB 485, Rep. Tiara Auxier (R). Cap on new-growth revenue. Never assigned to a committee.
HB 449 and HJR 20, Rep. Tiara Auxier (R). A taxpayer bill of rights: voter approval for tax and debt increases, a spending cap with refunds, sales-comparison assessment. Never assigned to a committee.
HB 365, Rep. Thomas Peterson (R). Entities must notice the amount and purpose of an increase before budgeting and cannot exceed it. Passed the      House 67-2, pulled into Senate Rules on March 4.
HB 170, Rep. Rex Shipp (R). School-board tax referendum, fourth year running. Passed the House 50-21, failed on the Senate floor 9-15.

This is not a state legislature that is your friend when it comes to taxpayer protections (and most of us can see that with our wallets and eyes). As the record shows, nearly every single time a legislator pushes common sense protections for you the taxpayer, they reject it, and usually in a humiliating fashion like denying it an assignment to a committee or letting it die without a sponsor in the Senate. For example, Tiara Auxier’s 2026 HB485 reasonable cap on new revenue growth was never even assigned to a committee for debate, and a taxpayer bill of rights she also sponsored (HB449), modeled after the very popular (with actual voters in both parties) Colorado Taxpayer Bill of Rights was also never even assigned to a committee. In sum, nearly every single chance this legislature has had to curb the growth of property, protect the taxpayer from the continued socialization of their taxes for the benefit of developers like Mike Kohlers HB128 in 2022 almost never even make it out of rules and into a committee, and those that do get killed elsewhere.

So the need that is so urgent to protect the taxpayer from themselves, as we’re being told by YES promoters, in my opinion is because they know they’ve boiled the frog on property taxes for too long. 

And this legislature through its own actions have created a true property tax crisis across the state by design, and they want to strip you of your ability to solve without them. Don’t trust me, don’t trust anyone, just look at the track records of those pushing it, and look at your own property tax bills as they’ve continued to push unfunded mandates and socialized benefits for developers like protecting them from impact fees as our middle-class and seniors get gouged each year. They do nothing, and even worse are desperate to prevent the frog they know is boiling on a potential citizen’s amendment on the issue from jumping out the pot to rescue us from their misdeeds that they have shown zero intention on ever fixing for us because it would finally force their developer donors to pay for their own burdens on the taxpayer.

This property tax crisis we’re in within Utah, is not unique to this state, and those who’ve studied the issue know that only very rarely do legislatures fix it voluntarily (powerful lobbies figure out ways to benefit from property taxes and fight hard to prevent changes), and in the vast majority of cases where true reform happened it was necessary for citizens to do it themselves (more on that below). But before we get into what we’re ultimately sacrificing as citizens if B passes, we first need to understand the language in this bill and why it is so pernicious, here’s the actual text:

"(iii) Notwithstanding Subsection (2)(a)(i)(A), initiated legislation that is subject to a vote that occurs after November 1, 2026, shall be adopted upon approval of at least 60% of those voting on the legislation if the initiated legislation includes:
(A) the imposition of a new tax;
(B) an expansion of an existing tax to include additional items or transactions subject to the tax;
(C) an increase in an existing tax rate; or
(D) for a property tax, a change to the tax rate that causes the tax rate to decrease less than it would under current law."

While this language seems innocuous it’s not. Let’s just say for example that on average the property tax rate was 0.6% and voters instead wanted to fix it at say 0.55% of cost rather than market value to permanently take back control of reasonableness from the tax authorities, then it would require a 60% vote even though the law is decreasing property taxes and structurally protecting the taxpayer against the madness that has happened over the past decade in Utah where we’ve been effectively socializing developer costs.

For example: values rise and the certified rate would fall from 0.6% to 0.5%. An initiative that holds the rate at 0.55%, or changes how new growth is counted so the math lands at 0.55%, “decreases less than it would under current law” and needs 60%, even though no one “raised” anything. This is the deception behind this language, which the sponsors are very aware of and hoping no one noticed how devastating this would be for any property tax reform effort by the citizens.

I believe this specific language, and the necessity to kneecap our ability to change the structure of said property taxes is at the core of why this was pushed and why it was pushed now. And to give you that same insight, it’s necessary to evaluate the progenitor of the bill, Senator Lincoln Fillmore, and the money behind the push for YES in the AFP-Utah.

Fillmore’s own admission that it “is not designed to stop any particular initiative,” and the sponsors’ “Highlighted Provisions” saying the target includes “the amount of revenue collected,” which is what makes clause (D) reach caps.

Let’s evaluate who Lincoln Fillmore and the AFP-Utah are truly working for, not by my declaration or your assumptions, but by the record. In 2026 alone, this bill’s sponsor Lincoln Fillmore, sponsored two other bills that in my opinion would’ve put gasoline on the trash fire that is the ongoing property tax crisis, including:

- SB245 (2026) – In committee, Mr. Fillmore moved to amend and advance a Musselman sponsored bill requiring cities to spend impact fees only on projects in the plan in place when the fees were collected. Homebuilders supported it, but fortunately for local taxpayer protections, it stalled on the Senate floor and died.
- HB184 (2026) – Mr. Fillmore was the Senate Sponsor of this monstrosity which was also actively lobbied for by the money behind this initiative The AFP-Utah. This bill would’ve significantly weakened local zoning that had provisions to automatically developer plans if so much as a local body did not respond formally within 45 days to such application. Needless to say, this bill would’ve exacerbated the property tax crisis by removing local councils from even having a say if they foot faulted on a builder application.

So to be clear, in 2026 alone Senator Fillmore pushed two bills, heavily lobbied for by the real industry, that would’ve been devastating to property taxpayers given the socialized nature of them in Utah (fortunately both were so bad that they died a quick death). But conveniently in this same session alongside his partner on HB184, the AFP-Utah, which is funding a good chunk of the money behind the YES on B effort, is pushing what I believe is a trojan horse amendment, that I show above does not offer the protections most voters think it does against out-of-state groups, and in reality solely kneecaps our own ability to take matters into our own hands vis-à-vis the growing property tax crisis in Utah. Property tax reform, by far, is the most likely use of a citizen-led effort in taxes in my opinion, and that’s what I believe they are protecting donors against.

In fact to make it even more real, the group that testified for SJR 2 (this Amendment B) at both hearings is the group that got the homeowner-exemption increase stripped from SJR 1 in 2023, whose opposition Koford cited for her 2025 and 2026 bills, and that told the Senate committee it preferred deferral to the circuit breaker. Its former president is the YES PAC’s spokesman. That is a provable chain from the YES lobby to blocked homeowner relief. So to be clear, the actual money behind this, that wants to protect you has actually lobbied to strip protections for homeowners, and did so recently.

So I’ll ask the voter, do you need protections from MWEG or rather from the actual proponents of YES per their own track record?

So what are we sacrificing in a real sense, that other states with similar issues (of tension between voters and lobbyists over property taxes), is the ability to solve the property tax crisis with initiatives. That is the voters’ ability to end the socialization of property taxes and put reasonable caps that allow our seniors and young families to financially plan their futures around, something not offered and actively blocked by our legislature.

Here are the States who were in similar spots to us with property tax crises that solved them (to the dismay of lobbyists who fought them every step of the way) in both red and blue states, and what B strips our ability as citizens to do ourselves:

Citizen initiatives that passed:
California, Prop 13 (1978). 1% rate cap, 2% assessment growth, reassessment only on sale, two-thirds for new taxes. The template.
Idaho, Proposition 1 (1978). A Prop 13 copy passed with 58%; the Legislature rewrote it into budget-growth limits within two years.
Michigan, Headlee Amendment (1978). Rolls millage rates back when assessments outrun inflation and requires voter approval for new local taxes.
Massachusetts, Proposition 2½ (1980). Levy capped at 2.5% of value and 2.5% annual      growth, overridable only by local vote. Still the backbone of      Massachusetts local finance.
Missouri, Hancock Amendment (1980). Revenue limit tied to personal income, levy rollbacks after reassessment, voter approval for local tax increases.
Montana, I-105 (1986). Froze property tax levies at 1986 levels.
Oregon, Measure 5 (1990) and Measure 47 (1996). Rate caps, then a rollback-and-3%-cap initiative that the Legislature replaced with Measure 50 (1997): a “maximum assessed value” that grows 3% a year regardless of  market value. This is the closest match to historical-cost-plus-3% model.
Florida, Save Our Homes (1992). Homestead assessments rise no more than 3% or CPI a year, whichever is lower.
Colorado, TABOR (1992). Voter approval for any tax increase, revenue limits with refunds.
Washington, I-747 (2001). Capped levy growth at 1% a year; the state supreme court struck it in 2007 and the Legislature re-enacted it in a special session      within weeks.

Legislature-referred amendments voters approved (noteworthy that this would still be at 50% in Utah, but because I believe only a threat of a voter amendment would get our legislature to back something similar as the record shows):
Alabama,  Amendment 373 (1978). Classification, assessment-ratio caps and mandatory votes on millage increases, passed in the Prop 13 panic.
Arizona, Prop 106 (1980) and Prop 117 (2012). A 1% cap on residential taxes, then a 5% cap on annual valuation growth.
Colorado,  Gallagher (1982). Fixed the residential share of the tax base, which drove the residential assessment rate from 21% to about 7%; voters      repealed it in 2020 (as “Amendment B,” oddly enough).
Michigan, Proposal A (1994). Taxable value grows no faster than inflation or 5%, resets on sale; school operating taxes shifted to a higher sales tax.
Oklahoma, SQ 676 (1996) and SQ 758 (2012). 5% cap on valuation growth, cut to 3% for homesteads and farmland.
Texas  (1997, 2023, 2025). 10% homestead appraisal cap, then a $100,000 homestead exemption with a 20% cap pilot for other property, then $140,000. Texas has no citizen initiative, so every one went through the Legislature.
Arkansas,  Amendment 79 (2000). 5% homestead and 10% other-property assessment caps plus a senior freeze.
South Carolina (2006). Reassessment increases capped at 15% over five years, paired with swapping school operating taxes on homes for a sales tax.
Florida, Amendment 1 (2008) and Amendment 5 (2024). Portability of the Save Our Homes cap and a 10% cap on non-homestead property, then an      inflation-indexed homestead exemption.
Indiana, Public Question 1 (2010). Wrote 1%, 2% and 3% caps on homes, other residential and business property into the constitution.
Georgia,  Amendment 1 (2024). Statewide homestead cap at inflation, with a local opt-out.
Wyoming, Amendment A (2024). Created a separate residential class so homes can be assessed differently; the 2025 Legislature then cut owner-occupied  assessments 25%.

So in sum, I know this post was dense, but given how this information doesn’t seem to be anywhere, I thought it necessary to put it all out for the public to see and scrutinize.

Powerful lobbyists know the property tax frog is reaching a boiling point and voters are near taking action as they have in so many other states previously and B effectively kills such efforts. It’s cynical, but with all the facts, in my opinion it’s the only logical conclusion given that the actual facts about protections against outside groups is just a smoke screen with no substance.

Lastly, please don’t interpret anything I write here as indicting any of B’s YES supporters as bad faith or they are in on it. 99% of people rallying behind the YES campaign are good faith actors that believe the narrative that they need to protected against outside groups and have not at all looked at the motives behind, nor fully understand its implications. This also includes the majority of our legislators who voted yes in the house and senate and like all the other bills had near zero time to evaluate its repercussions, and they should not be blamed as being “in on it”. I know some of them of them personally and they themselves were presented it the same way we have received info.

In my opinion, the biggest assist that YES has received is the fact that boogeyman groups the right uses to mobilize its base such as MWEG, and others have come out in the NO, which enables them to spin a left versus right narrative and distract from the actual facts that people who are good intentioned would have researched more thoroughly otherwise. I believe by tribalizing the issue, they’ve co-opted a lot of good people into buying the narrative that it’s us versus them, and them is the groups they want to defeat, letting their guard down against their “friends” who are funding the YES on B effort.

I’m hoping this note converts some of those folks and we can say no to concentrating more power into the hands of the legislature when it comes to our ability to reform property taxes. But it will take an army to make this succeed and it’s why I’m asking for your help in sharing this.

PLEASE SHARE WITH AS MANY AS POSSIBLE. YES IS UNFORNATELY AHEAD IN THE POLLS AND ONLY THROUGH A HERCULEAN GRASSROOTS EFFORT CAN WE SAVE OURSELVES FROM THIS LEGISLATIVE POWER GRAB, WHICH WILL MAKE NECESSARY PROPERTY TAX REFORM UNQUANTIFIABLY HARDER AND PERHAPS MAKE EVEN IMPOSSIBLE.

text:
**A U.S. Air Force service member died after falling while rappelling from the rafters of the Alamodome in San Antonio, Texas, during a pregame demonstration on Saturday, October 17, 2026.**

The incident occurred about 15 minutes before kickoff of the University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA) vs. Navy football game, which was designated as UTSA’s annual “Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans” game. Four service members from Detachment 2 of the 6th Combat Training Squadron (headquartered at Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, and operating from Joint Base San Antonio-Camp Bullis) were scheduled to rappel from the stadium rafters (roughly 150–170 feet above the field) onto the turf.

One of them, partway down, appeared to lose control, slid rapidly down the line in an uncontrolled manner, and crashed onto the field. Medical personnel and stadium staff immediately responded; he was treated on the field for about 10 minutes before being transported by stretcher (San Antonio Fire Department listed it as a Priority 1 / life-threatening case) to a local hospital, where he later died. The game was delayed roughly 10 minutes; UTSA went on to win 38–34 in front of about 23,000 fans.

Nellis Air Force Base Public Affairs confirmed the death. The service member’s name has not been released. The incident is under investigation. The 6th Combat Training Squadron Detachment 2 trains Tactical Air Control Party (TACP) specialists who embed with ground forces to direct air and artillery support; rappelling is part of their training.

UTSA President Taylor Eighmy and the university expressed deep sadness, offered condolences to the service member’s family and colleagues, and activated support services for the campus community. The American Conference also issued a statement of condolence.

This was a tragic accident during a military tribute intended to honor service members and veterans. Videos of the fall have circulated online, but major outlets have generally avoided sharing the most graphic footage.

Tesla’s Roadster reveal briefly sent crypto futures higher before the move reversed.

Tesla-linked perpetual futures on @Hyperliquid jumped to around $380 after Elon Musk unveiled the redesigned Roadster at SpaceX’s McGregor test facility in Texas. The contract then slid back toward $357, erasing the previous day’s gains after trading through a wide $360 to $380 range.

🚀→ $380 → $357

The move came with unusually large positioning behind it. Hyperliquid was carrying roughly $80 million in open interest, ahead of Binance at about $64.96 million. The contract is independently deployed and comes with the kind of conditions traders usually associate with thinner synthetic markets: lower liquidity, fast repricing and higher liquidation sensitivity.

Across venues, the reaction was broadly negative:

Binance TSLAUSDT: $357.26, -0.85%
OKX: -0.84%
Lighter: -1.30%
Hyperliquid: back near $357 after touching $380

The Roadster presentation itself leaned heavily into engineering spectacle. Musk showed a thruster-equipped version developed with input from Tesla and SpaceX engineers, reviving a product that has been delayed for years and now carries a production target roughly eight years beyond the original schedule announced in 2017.

The market response matters because these Tesla-linked perpetuals are increasingly functioning as a 24/7 sentiment layer around corporate events, especially outside regular U.S. trading hours. 

They are still small compared with traditional equity derivatives, but they offer a much faster view into speculative positioning around companies with strong retail followings.

@Tesla reports third-quarter results after the close on Oct. 21, followed by management Q&A at 5:30 p.m. ET. Until then, the contract remains well below the Roadster spike, with traders back around the mid-$350s.

What actually exists:
• TDHCA and TSAHC offer down-payment assistance as a 0% second lien (usually 2–5%). The primary mortgage is a normal market-rate FHA/VA/USDA/conventional loan. These follow federal residency rules—undocumented immigrants generally don’t qualify.
• Local Habitat for Humanity affiliates sometimes offer true 0% mortgages, but they require U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, income limits, and hundreds of hours of sweat equity.
• Undocumented immigrants can buy homes in Texas with private ITIN loans. Those usually require higher down payments and higher interest rates. They are not taxpayer-subsidized zero-interest products.

Historically, mobile development meant compromised emergency hotfixes on tiny screens. Smart phones are too cramped for wide code diffs, while laptops demand lap space and flat desks. The iPad—with its brilliant retina display, instant wake, and fluid touch ecosystem—bridges human strategic intuition and heavy desktop computation seamlessly.

2. Grix iPad-to-Desktop Orchestration Architecture

Grix establishes a dedicated tablet protocol connecting your iPad directly to the Cursor runtime on your Mac:

tablet_orchestration_hub:

Phase 1: Canvas Scoping: Frame objectives on iPad and route tickets to desktop workers;

Phase 3: Real-Time Tablet Telemetry: Live test logs, coverage bars, and security reports stream to your tablet glass;

Transform your iPad from a passive entertainment slate into a high-leverage mobile command center. With Grix orchestrating desktop Cursor, complex engineering becomes an ambient, untethered reality.

text:
On Sunday, we are reminded of God’s global work.

Sometimes we recognize God's work through stories of a new church, a baptism, or someone deciding to follow Jesus. Other times, His work becomes visible through a physical therapist helping a child, a teacher reopening a classroom, or a national believer preparing Scripture in a language their community understands.

These stories remind us that the Great Commission needs more than people willing to go overseas. It needs people willing to use what God has entrusted to them.

But what happens when Sunday is over?

We wake up on Monday, grab our coffee, and head to work. Our attention shifts to emails, deadlines, meetings, and everything waiting for us.

And somewhere in the busyness, we can forget that God is at work there, too.

Serving the Lord isn't just a Sunday thing.

Think about it. You may spend 40 hours a week at your job, surrounded by people God has placed in your life.

You were hired because you have certain skills, but as a follower of Jesus, you have something more to offer.

An opportunity to encourage someone going through a difficult season.

A conversation over lunch about faith.

An invitation to church or a Bible study.

Or simply doing your work with integrity and kindness in a way that reflects Christ.

There are people right where you work who need to know the hope found in Jesus.

So this Monday, consider walking into work with a different perspective.

It's not just missionaries and pastors who are called to serve.

God can use you right where you are, with the skills He's given you and the people He's placed around you.

What would change about your Monday if you began seeing your workplace as an opportunity for ministry?

text:
October 11 Saint Tarachus (Tharacus, Tracio) and his Companions: Martyrs
died  304
.
During the persecution of Diocletian in the year 304, Tarachus, Probus, and Andronicus, differing in age and nationality but united in the bonds of faith, were denounced as Christians to the governor of Cilicia. They were arrested at Pompeiopolis, and conducted to Tarsus. The acts of these glorious martyrs are one of the most precious monuments of Church history. The interrogations, making up the first three parts of their acts, were recorded in the proconsular registers, which the Christians bought for 200 denari from the public Notary. Line by line, we read the questions posed by the governor of Cilicia named Maximus, and the answers of the martyrs. These are followed by a narration of their death, written by three Christian eyewitnesses, Mark, Felix and Verus, who buried their bodies.
.
Tarachus was a retired military officer of the imperial armies, who had reached the age of sixty-five. Probus had abandoned a fortune to serve Jesus Christ with greater liberty. Andronicus, the youngest, was a member of one of the first families of Ephesus.
.
When Tarachus was told to sacrifice, he replied, I cannot renounce the law of God. The governor of the province said, There is only one law, the one we obey.
.
Tarachus: There is another, and you transgress it by adoring your own handiwork, statues of wood or stone. He was struck on the mouth and beaten with rods. Tarachus said while being struck: Now you are making me truly wise; the blows you give me fortify me, they increase my confidence in God and in Jesus Christ. He was chained and taken to prison.
.
Probus was no less courageous; while he was being beaten the governor said to him, Look at your torn body, wretch, and the ground covered with your blood!
.
Probus: The more my flesh suffers for Jesus Christ, the more my soul acquires strength and vigor. He was placed in irons and no one was permitted to dress his wounds.
.
When the turn of Andronicus came, Maximus said to him: Adore the gods and obey the emperors, who are our fathers and masters.
Andronicus: The devil is your father, when you do his works.
.
Maximus: Young man, you are insolent; do you know that I have torments in readiness?
.
Andronicus: I would rather see my body cut into pieces than lose my soul.
.
Maximus: Wretch, we will see if you are insensible to torments. When you feel them, you will perhaps renounce your folly.
.
Andronicus: This folly is advantageous for us who hope in Jesus Christ. The wisdom of the world leads to eternal death. He was tortured on the rack, and salt put on his wounds. He said: Your torments have procured true refreshment for my body.
.
Maximus: I will have you perish by a slow death. And he had him chained like the others and put in prison.
.
A short time later they were moved to another city, where the same governor began the questioning over again. Tarachus had his teeth broken, his hands burnt, and vinegar and salt poured into his nostrils. He said: Your vinegar has only sweetness for me, and your salt seems insipid to me. Probus, brought before him, told him, My soul is stronger than ever. In heaven I have a living God whom I serve and adore; I know no other. When told to sacrifice to Jupiter, he said, Can you give the name of god to one soiled by adulteries, incests, and other enormous crimes? And when struck on the mouth, he said, I have not injured truth, I only said of Jupiter what all who adore him already know. He was burnt with hot coals on the head and feet. Andronicus was led before Maximus and told that his companions had ceded under torture. He answered: Why do you try to deceive me? My companions have not renounced the cult of the true God, and even if they had, I would not commit such an impiety. The God I adore has given me the arms of faith. Jesus Christ, my Saviour, is my strength, in such wise that I do not dread your power or that of your masters or that of your gods. You can test me with all the tortures that the most refined cruelty suggests to you. He was again beaten and salt was rubbed into his wounds. Maximus said to him: You will not despise my authority with impunity.
.
Andronicus: It will not be said, either, that the cause of Jesus Christ has succumbed under your authority.
.
A third interrogation and another series of tortures followed at still another city. Tarachus was cruelly tortured; when his ears were cut off he only said: My heart is no less attentive to the word of God, and made other similar replies, as respectful as they were heroic. Maximus said to Probus: The God you invoke has delivered you Himself into my hands.
.
Probus: He loves men. Food offered to idols was forced into his mouth.
.
Probus: I have abandoned my body to your power in order to save my soul. When you force me to eat what has been offered on your abominable altars, I am not soiled; God is witness to the violence I suffer. He was blinded. He replied: You have deprived me of the eyes of the body, but cannot take from me those of the soul. If you knew your own blindness, you would find you were more unfortunate than I am. The youngest confessor had his teeth pulled out, and was told he would be devoured by the beasts in the amphitheater. He said: God will deliver me when it so pleases Him.
.
Unable to walk because of their wounds, these disciples of Christ were borne to the amphitheater. The wild animals, when released, would not approach the martyrs; a bear who had killed three men that day, came and licked the feet of the youngest martyr. The governor had the beast killed. A furious lioness, even after being provoked, lay down at the feet of Tarachus and licked them. Gladiators were told to kill the martyrs. The Christians of the city sent this narration to the church of Iconium, telling them to make it known to the faithful of the other cities of the region for their edification.
.
Reflection: Such is true Christian devotion. Is ours the faith of the Apostles who cried: Neither death nor life shall be able to separate us from the love that is in Christ Jesus? (Cf. Romans 8:38-39)
.
Eternal Father, I wish to honor Saint Tarachus and his Companions, and I give Thee thanks for all the graces Thou hast bestowed upon them. I ask Thee to please increase grace in my soul through the merits of this saint, and I commit the end of my life to them by this special prayer, so that by virtue of Thy goodness and promise, Saint Tarachus and his Companions might be my advocate and provide whatever is needed at that hour. Amen.

text:
CONSERVATIVE FRIENDS: PLEASE READ BEFORE VOTING ON AMENDMENT B.
tl;dr: this is a battle for control over of your property taxes, and the ability to continue socializing them for donors, and I believe powerful interests are getting in front of any effort to reform this broken system as was necessary in 20 other states who had similar issues before and where voters finally took action. I do not believe a good faith reading has anything to do with protecting you from outside groups wanting to raise taxes (the record below shows that). Further, even if a tax pass through initiative, the State Legislature retains the ability to immediately repeal it before it ever taxes anyone, meaning the benefits being sold are illusory. Instead, I believe lobbyists for developers and their preferred legislators are the progenitors of this initiative and behind this campaign inn a pre-emptive attempt from stopping their looting of our property taxes. Please vote NO, so we can right the wrongs the legislature has given us vis-à-vis socialized costs and private profits for their donors, and as is demonstrated below any property tax restructuring will almost certainly require a 60% vote per this Amendment. They know the political winds are turning hard on property taxes and this bill is designed to frustrate any citizen led effort on the topic. All the receipts are below, please read and share this post as time is short to beat back this bad faith Amendment.
----------
The claims:
With that out of the way, let’s evaluate the claims as being presented by the legislature and its big money backers to voters.

The first and most obvious is that, despite your lying eyes of being in the highest taxed red state, they’re desperate to protect you from higher taxes. And that groups like MWEG have ulterior motives to further increase the highest tax burden of any red state, and the threat was so severe that it necessitates a constitutional amendment in 2026. Let’s evaluate the evidence to assess how real this threat is in 2026:

· “Out-of-state special interest money”(Rep. Blake Moore, Hesterman, AFP). Amendment B limits votes, not money. Utah has no contribution limits at all, and the legislature refuses to change this. And the YES side’s own organizations on Ballotpedia’s list are Americans for Prosperity–Utah and Americans for Tax Reform, both national groups
· “You can’t vote out your neighbors.” You don’t need to; the Legislature rewrote all three 2018 initiatives by simple majority (Prop 2 in December 2018, Prop 3 in February 2019, Prop 4 in 2020). Voters have no such recourse against the Legislature’s tax votes.
· “It protects taxpayers.” From voters, and in name only. The Legislature raises taxes on a simple majority with no public vote, and in 2018 it froze the school property tax levy, about $125 million a year in increases nobody voted on. Rep. Dailey-Provost’s offer to apply 60% to legislators went nowhere.

And countervailing all this is the hysteria by its proponents about boogeyman left wing groups is that any tax increase, can be undone by a simple legislative majority, period. So, all this nonsense about your legislators being the only officials you can trust is not credible, and I’d characterize it in some cases as bad faith gaslighting in some cases, but in most cases it’s good people that have been co-opted by a deceptive narrative being spun by those with undisclosed agendas at work.

And before someone addresses it in the comments, I want to point out that the 2024 Supreme Court ruling on initiatives does not at all cover taxation, so constitutionally, any tax some left-wing group pushed (as the sponsors tell us we need to protect against), could be repealed by a simple majority in the legislature.

So if there exists no known initiative this is meant to counter (per the Sponsors’ own admissions), and also in reality does not even preclude the legislature from undoing a bad initiative voters were duped into voting for, then what exactly is going on here with this massive push with money from out-of-state lobbyists such as the AFP-Utah to desperately get us to take away our ability to influence our taxation?

Hint, it has everything to do with the continued socialization of your property taxes for the benefit of developers.

But before getting into the practical consequences of how devastating this 60% threshold will be against a potential reform movement, let’s talk about the track record of those in the legislature trying to protect us against these invisible tax boogeyman over the past 5 years. Nearly every single time a bill came up to curb the ability to raise taxes, give us a bill of rights, or otherwise protect us from developers who’ve figured out how to prime us for their private profits, the legislature has rejected it, and here are the receipts:

2022
HB478, Rep. Brad Last (R). Ended the school basic-levy freeze a year early and repealed the WPU value rate. Passed the House 56-13, died in Senate Rules.
HB128, Rep. Mike Kohler (R). Repealed the 1995 school impact fee ban so districts could charge impact fees. Never assigned to a committee.

2023
HB260, Rep. Joel Briscoe (D). Raised the circuit breaker income cap to $50,000. Passed the House 68-0, pulled into Senate Rules; the Senate tax chair said he preferred deferral.
HB454, Rep. Kera Birkeland (R). Senior cap: taxes could rise no more than 5% a year for homeowners 70+ under $50,000 income. Listed in committee, never considered.
HB296, Rep. Walt Brooks (R) and SB 141, Sen. Wayne Harper (R). Cut the statewide school levy by $100M–$128M. Neither was ever assigned to a      committee.
SJR1, Sen. Dan McCay (R). Would have let the Legislature exempt more than 45% of home value. The committee stripped that language after Utah      Taxpayers Association opposition; the remainder died in House Rules.
HB298, Rep. Candice Pierucci (R). Full primary-residence exemption for 100%-disabled veterans. Died in House Rules.
HB372, Rep. James Cobb (R). Let voters refer school-board tax increases to the ballot. On the agenda, never discussed.

2024
HB354, Rep. Tyler Clancy (R). Voter approval before any entity exceeds its certified rate through 2026. Never heard.
HB173, Rep. Candice Pierucci (R). School-board tax referendum. Passed the House 42-28; the Senate committee listed it and skipped it.
HB512, Rep. Walt Brooks (R). Cut the school levy by $75M. Never assigned to a committee.
SB146, Sen. Keith Grover (R). Senior and disabled “work-off” credit against property tax. Never heard.

2025
SB224, Sen. Wayne Harper (R). Raised the circuit breaker limit to $46,000 and the top credit to $2,000. Never assigned to a committee.
HJR7 and HB428, Rep. Jill Koford (R). Raise the primary residential exemption to 50%, with constitutional room to 55%. HJR 7 never left Rules;      the 50% was stripped from HB 428 before passage.
HB511, Rep. Tiara Auxier (R). Voter opinion question before revenue increases, plus a cap on retained new-growth revenue. Held in committee      9-0.
HB 408, Rep. Rex Shipp (R). School-board referendum including tax increases. Passed the House 40-33, failed in Senate committee 3-4.

2026
SB97, Sen. Dan McCay (R). As filed, a 5% cap on Truth-in-Taxation increases; rewritten into fund-balance limits and a one-exemption-per-household rule. Died on the Senate floor 14-15.
HJR 7 and HB 161, Rep. Jill Koford (R). Primary residential exemption to 60%. Assigned to committee, never heard; Koford cited business opposition.
HB 484, Rep. Kay Christofferson (R). 5% cap on Truth-in-Taxation revenue growth unless voters approve more. Held in committee 7-3 after two hours of testimony.
HB 485, Rep. Tiara Auxier (R). Cap on new-growth revenue. Never assigned to a committee.
HB 449 and HJR 20, Rep. Tiara Auxier (R). A taxpayer bill of rights: voter approval for tax and debt increases, a spending cap with refunds, sales-comparison assessment. Never assigned to a committee.
HB 365, Rep. Thomas Peterson (R). Entities must notice the amount and purpose of an increase before budgeting and cannot exceed it. Passed the      House 67-2, pulled into Senate Rules on March 4.
HB 170, Rep. Rex Shipp (R). School-board tax referendum, fourth year running. Passed the House 50-21, failed on the Senate floor 9-15.

This is not a state legislature that is your friend when it comes to taxpayer protections (and most of us can see that with our wallets and eyes). As the record shows, nearly every single time a legislator pushes common sense protections for you the taxpayer, they reject it, and usually in a humiliating fashion like denying it an assignment to a committee or letting it die without a sponsor in the Senate. For example, Tiara Auxier’s 2026 HB485 reasonable cap on new revenue growth was never even assigned to a committee for debate, and a taxpayer bill of rights she also sponsored (HB449), modeled after the very popular (with actual voters in both parties) Colorado Taxpayer Bill of Rights was also never even assigned to a committee. In sum, nearly every single chance this legislature has had to curb the growth of property, protect the taxpayer from the continued socialization of their taxes for the benefit of developers like Mike Kohlers HB128 in 2022 almost never even make it out of rules and into a committee, and those that do get killed elsewhere.

So the need that is so urgent to protect the taxpayer from themselves, as we’re being told by YES promoters, in my opinion is because they know they’ve boiled the frog on property taxes for too long. 

And this legislature through its own actions have created a true property tax crisis across the state by design, and they want to strip you of your ability to solve without them. Don’t trust me, don’t trust anyone, just look at the track records of those pushing it, and look at your own property tax bills as they’ve continued to push unfunded mandates and socialized benefits for developers like protecting them from impact fees as our middle-class and seniors get gouged each year. They do nothing, and even worse are desperate to prevent the frog they know is boiling on a potential citizen’s amendment on the issue from jumping out the pot to rescue us from their misdeeds that they have shown zero intention on ever fixing for us because it would finally force their developer donors to pay for their own burdens on the taxpayer.

This property tax crisis we’re in within Utah, is not unique to this state, and those who’ve studied the issue know that only very rarely do legislatures fix it voluntarily (powerful lobbies figure out ways to benefit from property taxes and fight hard to prevent changes), and in the vast majority of cases where true reform happened it was necessary for citizens to do it themselves (more on that below). But before we get into what we’re ultimately sacrificing as citizens if B passes, we first need to understand the language in this bill and why it is so pernicious, here’s the actual text:

"(iii) Notwithstanding Subsection (2)(a)(i)(A), initiated legislation that is subject to a vote that occurs after November 1, 2026, shall be adopted upon approval of at least 60% of those voting on the legislation if the initiated legislation includes:
(A) the imposition of a new tax;
(B) an expansion of an existing tax to include additional items or transactions subject to the tax;
(C) an increase in an existing tax rate; or
(D) for a property tax, a change to the tax rate that causes the tax rate to decrease less than it would under current law."

While this language seems innocuous it’s not. Let’s just say for example that on average the property tax rate was 0.6% and voters instead wanted to fix it at say 0.55% of cost rather than market value to permanently take back control of reasonableness from the tax authorities, then it would require a 60% vote even though the law is decreasing property taxes and structurally protecting the taxpayer against the madness that has happened over the past decade in Utah where we’ve been effectively socializing developer costs.

For example: values rise and the certified rate would fall from 0.6% to 0.5%. An initiative that holds the rate at 0.55%, or changes how new growth is counted so the math lands at 0.55%, “decreases less than it would under current law” and needs 60%, even though no one “raised” anything. This is the deception behind this language, which the sponsors are very aware of and hoping no one noticed how devastating this would be for any property tax reform effort by the citizens.

I believe this specific language, and the necessity to kneecap our ability to change the structure of said property taxes is at the core of why this was pushed and why it was pushed now. And to give you that same insight, it’s necessary to evaluate the progenitor of the bill, Senator Lincoln Fillmore, and the money behind the push for YES in the AFP-Utah.

Fillmore’s own admission that it “is not designed to stop any particular initiative,” and the sponsors’ “Highlighted Provisions” saying the target includes “the amount of revenue collected,” which is what makes clause (D) reach caps.

Let’s evaluate who Lincoln Fillmore and the AFP-Utah are truly working for, not by my declaration or your assumptions, but by the record. In 2026 alone, this bill’s sponsor Lincoln Fillmore, sponsored two other bills that in my opinion would’ve put gasoline on the trash fire that is the ongoing property tax crisis, including:

- SB245 (2026) – In committee, Mr. Fillmore moved to amend and advance a Musselman sponsored bill requiring cities to spend impact fees only on projects in the plan in place when the fees were collected. Homebuilders supported it, but fortunately for local taxpayer protections, it stalled on the Senate floor and died.
- HB184 (2026) – Mr. Fillmore was the Senate Sponsor of this monstrosity which was also actively lobbied for by the money behind this initiative The AFP-Utah. This bill would’ve significantly weakened local zoning that had provisions to automatically developer plans if so much as a local body did not respond formally within 45 days to such application. Needless to say, this bill would’ve exacerbated the property tax crisis by removing local councils from even having a say if they foot faulted on a builder application.

So to be clear, in 2026 alone Senator Fillmore pushed two bills, heavily lobbied for by the real industry, that would’ve been devastating to property taxpayers given the socialized nature of them in Utah (fortunately both were so bad that they died a quick death). But conveniently in this same session alongside his partner on HB184, the AFP-Utah, which is funding a good chunk of the money behind the YES on B effort, is pushing what I believe is a trojan horse amendment, that I show above does not offer the protections most voters think it does against out-of-state groups, and in reality solely kneecaps our own ability to take matters into our own hands vis-à-vis the growing property tax crisis in Utah. Property tax reform, by far, is the most likely use of a citizen-led effort in taxes in my opinion, and that’s what I believe they are protecting donors against.

In fact to make it even more real, the group that testified for SJR 2 (this Amendment B) at both hearings is the group that got the homeowner-exemption increase stripped from SJR 1 in 2023, whose opposition Koford cited for her 2025 and 2026 bills, and that told the Senate committee it preferred deferral to the circuit breaker. Its former president is the YES PAC’s spokesman. That is a provable chain from the YES lobby to blocked homeowner relief. So to be clear, the actual money behind this, that wants to protect you has actually lobbied to strip protections for homeowners, and did so recently.

So I’ll ask the voter, do you need protections from MWEG or rather from the actual proponents of YES per their own track record?

So what are we sacrificing in a real sense, that other states with similar issues (of tension between voters and lobbyists over property taxes), is the ability to solve the property tax crisis with initiatives. That is the voters’ ability to end the socialization of property taxes and put reasonable caps that allow our seniors and young families to financially plan their futures around, something not offered and actively blocked by our legislature.

Here are the States who were in similar spots to us with property tax crises that solved them (to the dismay of lobbyists who fought them every step of the way) in both red and blue states, and what B strips our ability as citizens to do ourselves:

Citizen initiatives that passed:
California, Prop 13 (1978). 1% rate cap, 2% assessment growth, reassessment only on sale, two-thirds for new taxes. The template.
Idaho, Proposition 1 (1978). A Prop 13 copy passed with 58%; the Legislature rewrote it into budget-growth limits within two years.
Michigan, Headlee Amendment (1978). Rolls millage rates back when assessments outrun inflation and requires voter approval for new local taxes.
Massachusetts, Proposition 2½ (1980). Levy capped at 2.5% of value and 2.5% annual      growth, overridable only by local vote. Still the backbone of      Massachusetts local finance.
Missouri, Hancock Amendment (1980). Revenue limit tied to personal income, levy rollbacks after reassessment, voter approval for local tax increases.
Montana, I-105 (1986). Froze property tax levies at 1986 levels.
Oregon, Measure 5 (1990) and Measure 47 (1996). Rate caps, then a rollback-and-3%-cap initiative that the Legislature replaced with Measure 50 (1997): a “maximum assessed value” that grows 3% a year regardless of  market value. This is the closest match to historical-cost-plus-3% model.
Florida, Save Our Homes (1992). Homestead assessments rise no more than 3% or CPI a year, whichever is lower.
Colorado, TABOR (1992). Voter approval for any tax increase, revenue limits with refunds.
Washington, I-747 (2001). Capped levy growth at 1% a year; the state supreme court struck it in 2007 and the Legislature re-enacted it in a special session      within weeks.

Legislature-referred amendments voters approved (noteworthy that this would still be at 50% in Utah, but because I believe only a threat of a voter amendment would get our legislature to back something similar as the record shows):
Alabama,  Amendment 373 (1978). Classification, assessment-ratio caps and mandatory votes on millage increases, passed in the Prop 13 panic.
Arizona, Prop 106 (1980) and Prop 117 (2012). A 1% cap on residential taxes, then a 5% cap on annual valuation growth.
Colorado,  Gallagher (1982). Fixed the residential share of the tax base, which drove the residential assessment rate from 21% to about 7%; voters      repealed it in 2020 (as “Amendment B,” oddly enough).
Michigan, Proposal A (1994). Taxable value grows no faster than inflation or 5%, resets on sale; school operating taxes shifted to a higher sales tax.
Oklahoma, SQ 676 (1996) and SQ 758 (2012). 5% cap on valuation growth, cut to 3% for homesteads and farmland.
Texas  (1997, 2023, 2025). 10% homestead appraisal cap, then a $100,000 homestead exemption with a 20% cap pilot for other property, then $140,000. Texas has no citizen initiative, so every one went through the Legislature.
Arkansas,  Amendment 79 (2000). 5% homestead and 10% other-property assessment caps plus a senior freeze.
South Carolina (2006). Reassessment increases capped at 15% over five years, paired with swapping school operating taxes on homes for a sales tax.
Florida, Amendment 1 (2008) and Amendment 5 (2024). Portability of the Save Our Homes cap and a 10% cap on non-homestead property, then an      inflation-indexed homestead exemption.
Indiana, Public Question 1 (2010). Wrote 1%, 2% and 3% caps on homes, other residential and business property into the constitution.
Georgia,  Amendment 1 (2024). Statewide homestead cap at inflation, with a local opt-out.
Wyoming, Amendment A (2024). Created a separate residential class so homes can be assessed differently; the 2025 Legislature then cut owner-occupied  assessments 25%.

So in sum, I know this post was dense, but given how this information doesn’t seem to be anywhere, I thought it necessary to put it all out for the public to see and scrutinize.

Powerful lobbyists know the property tax frog is reaching a boiling point and voters are near taking action as they have in so many other states previously and B effectively kills such efforts. It’s cynical, but with all the facts, in my opinion it’s the only logical conclusion given that the actual facts about protections against outside groups is just a smoke screen with no substance.

Lastly, please don’t interpret anything I write here as indicting any of B’s YES supporters as bad faith or they are in on it. 99% of people rallying behind the YES campaign are good faith actors that believe the narrative that they need to protected against outside groups and have not at all looked at the motives behind, nor fully understand its implications. This also includes the majority of our legislators who voted yes in the house and senate and like all the other bills had near zero time to evaluate its repercussions, and they should not be blamed as being “in on it”. I know some of them of them personally and they themselves were presented it the same way we have received info.

In my opinion, the biggest assist that YES has received is the fact that boogeyman groups the right uses to mobilize its base such as MWEG, and others have come out in the NO, which enables them to spin a left versus right narrative and distract from the actual facts that people who are good intentioned would have researched more thoroughly otherwise. I believe by tribalizing the issue, they’ve co-opted a lot of good people into buying the narrative that it’s us versus them, and them is the groups they want to defeat, letting their guard down against their “friends” who are funding the YES on B effort.

I’m hoping this note converts some of those folks and we can say no to concentrating more power into the hands of the legislature when it comes to our ability to reform property taxes. But it will take an army to make this succeed and it’s why I’m asking for your help in sharing this.

PLEASE SHARE WITH AS MANY AS POSSIBLE. YES IS UNFORNATELY AHEAD IN THE POLLS AND ONLY THROUGH A HERCULEAN GRASSROOTS EFFORT CAN WE SAVE OURSELVES FROM THIS LEGISLATIVE POWER GRAB, WHICH WILL MAKE NECESSARY PROPERTY TAX REFORM UNQUANTIFIABLY HARDER AND PERHAPS MAKE EVEN IMPOSSIBLE.

The bridesmaids, stunning in dusty blue gowns, kept the energy high as everyone embraced the weather, running through the raindrops and creating candid, joyful memories that will last a lifetime.

text:
Why Your Holster Choice Is a Life-or-Death Decision for Church Security

In 2025, three churches were struck by active shooters. The one with trained, armed volunteers lost zero congregation members. The other two lost 42 people combined. That contrast is not a coincidence. It is the result of preparation, training, and purpose-built gear.

According to Christian Warrior Training's analysis of the FBI 2025 Active Shooter Report, 3 of 34 active shooter incidents occurred at churches. That is just 9% of total events, yet those three attacks produced 43 of the nation's 166 total casualties: 26% of all deaths. Churches are disproportionately lethal targets.

The threat is accelerating. Church attacks surged nearly 900% from 2018 to 2023, and gun-related incidents more than doubled from 12 to 28 between 2023 and 2024, according to the Family Research Council via Daily Citizen. A 2023 Lifeway Research survey found that 54% of Protestant churches recruiting security volunteers arm them, making armed congregant volunteers the dominant model over professional guards. Yet roughly 50% of those volunteers are civilians with limited formal tactical training. Gear selection is not a preference. It is a component of a life-safety system.

The Theological Foundation: Called to Protect

Romans 13:4 frames the armed protector as "God's servant for your good" and "an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer." For church security volunteers, this is not metaphor. It is a direct theological mandate for the sheepdog role within a congregation.

C&G Holsters is a Christian-owned company, founded by a retired Law Enforcement Officer and Master Firearms Instructor. We engrave Romans 13:4 on every holster we produce. That is not a marketing decision. It is a statement of who we are and what we believe the protector's role demands.

The sheepdog role within a congregation is a calling, not merely a volunteer slot on a signup sheet. On June 22, 2025, volunteer security members at CrossPointe Community Church in Wayne, Michigan proved that calling in action. An attacker carrying an AR-15 and a handgun attempted to enter a Sunday service with 150+ worshippers inside. Trained, armed volunteers stopped him before he reached the congregation. Zero parishioners died, as reported by the Crime Prevention Research Center. Duty and faith are not in conflict. They are unified in the church security volunteer mission.

Know Your Environment: Where Church Violence Actually Happens

Most people picture an active shooter bursting through sanctuary doors mid-sermon. The data tells a different story. According to Christian Warrior Training's 2025 tracking data, over 70% of violent incidents at churches occurred outside the building, in parking lots and on church grounds, not inside the sanctuary during services.

That single statistic reshapes every gear decision you make. Your holster must perform equally well while you are seated in a pew for 90 minutes and while you are patrolling a parking lot in dress clothes. These are two fundamentally different physical demands, and your gear must handle both.

The Family Research Council tracked 415 hostile incidents targeting U.S. churches in 2024 alone, the second-highest annual total ever recorded, spanning 383 churches across 43 states. In 2025, 23 of 34 active shooters (68%) showed predatory, pre-planned behavior. They scouted. They prepared. That pattern underscores the value of threat recognition during pre-service parking lot patrol, where an alert volunteer can identify warning signs before an attacker ever reaches the door.

Meanwhile, Omnilert reports that 17% of Protestant churches still have zero security measures: no armed personnel, no radio, no active shooter plan. In most congregations, volunteer teams are the last line of defense. Gear must be selected for a dual-environment role: formal indoor concealment and active outdoor patrol posture.

Carry Position: Matching Draw to the Church Environment

Appendix carry (AIWB) offers the highest concealment ceiling of any carry position. When you bend, squat, or sit in a pew, an AIWB holster stays tucked against your body where strong-side options can print or shift. For volunteers who sit through full services, AIWB is the top choice.

Strong-side IWB at 3:30 to 4 o'clock is the best balance of concealment and comfort for extended multi-hour wear in formal attire. Strong-side carry distributes weight naturally along the beltline, making it the preferred alternative for volunteers who find AIWB uncomfortable during seated services.

Here is a critical training gap most teams overlook: the majority of church security volunteers have never practiced drawing from a seated pew position. Dry-fire rehearsal from a seated posture, in the clothes you will actually wear, must happen before any live assignment.

Parking lot patrol changes the equation. Strong-side carry allows a more natural draw during standing movement. AIWB requires deliberate practice to access efficiently while walking. OWB carry under a sport coat or suit jacket is viable for patrol-heavy roles, but it demands a well-fitted cover garment. Any printing defeats the concealment mission.

One final rule: carry position must be chosen once and trained consistently. Switching positions between indoor and outdoor phases of a service creates dangerous muscle-memory confusion. Pick one position, train it under every scenario you will encounter, and commit to it.

Retention Level: Choosing Level I, II, or III for Your Role

Level I passive retention (friction-fit Kydex, IWB or OWB) is the appropriate standard for concealed church security volunteers. It allows a clean, consistent draw without secondary retention devices that slow response time under stress. When fractions of a second determine outcomes, simplicity wins.

Level II retention is recommended if the volunteer carries openly, patrols high-traffic exterior areas, or may engage in physical confrontations where weapon retention becomes a direct concern. The added retention device (typically a thumb release or hood) provides security against a grab attempt, which matters more in an exposed patrol role than in a concealed one.

Level III retention is generally inappropriate for civilian concealed roles. The added draw complexity under stress, often requiring three distinct release motions, outweighs the retention benefit in a plainclothes church environment. Retention level is a function of role, not a status symbol.

CCW Safe training data confirms that some holsters used by church security volunteers do not lend themselves to concealed carry, and others are outright dangerous during reholstering. Passive Kydex with a defined retention click eliminates both risks. You hear and feel the firearm lock into place. Every time.

Concealed volunteers should prioritize draw speed. Patrol volunteers should prioritize weapon security. Match your retention level to your specific role, attire, and likely threat scenario.

Our COVERT and ALPHA Kydex holster lines, available in both IWB and OWB configurations with Quickship (5-day) and fully custom options, are CNC-machined from custom aluminum molds to deliver consistent, repeatable draw with Level I passive retention built for the concealed civilian role. The COVERT IWB is particularly well-suited for AIWB and strong-side church carry in formal attire, with low-profile clips and optional claw/wing attachments for maximum concealment.

Concealment in Formal Church Attire: The Plainclothes Challenge

Church security volunteers must look like congregants, not operators. Printing, visible clips, or tactical gear immediately compromise the concealment mission and may actually escalate a threat by identifying you as the first target.

Dress shirts and slacks require a holster with a low-profile clip and a wing or claw attachment. The wing presses against the inside of your belt, rotating the grip inward and reducing printing against thinner dress fabric. Without it, even a compact firearm can telegraph its outline through a tucked shirt.

Sport coats and suit jackets are the most effective cover garments for OWB or strong-side IWB carry. The volunteer must practice drawing from a buttoned jacket under time pressure. Fumbling with a button under stress is a training problem, not a gear problem, and it must be solved before the first live assignment.

Tucked-shirt carry requires a dedicated tuckable IWB holster with clips that disappear under a tucked dress shirt. Not all Kydex holsters support this configuration, so verify compatibility before purchasing.

Belt selection is non-negotiable. A rigid gun belt, 1.5-inch minimum width, is required to support a holstered firearm through a 2 to 3 hour service without shift or sag. A standard dress belt will fail under the weight, shifting and sagging until it compromises your draw.

Multi-hour wear in formal attire is a unique physical demand. Conduct a full dress rehearsal at home before your first live assignment. Wear the exact outfit, holster, belt, and firearm for the full duration of a typical service. Identify hotspots, printing issues, and draw interference before they matter.

Medical Integration: The IFAK Is Not Optional

Church security experts now argue that if a safety team carries only one category of equipment beyond communication, it should be medical gear. Trace Armory Group and other industry voices are clear: a compact IFAK with a tourniquet, hemostatic gauze, and chest seal belongs on every volunteer's belt.

The skills gap is real. In a randomized trial of 465 laypeople cited by MED-TAC International, only 16% of untrained individuals applied a tourniquet correctly. After a one-hour ACS Bleeding Control Basic course, that number jumped to 88%. Retention dropped to 54.5% at 3 to 9 months without refresher training. Tourniquet skills require regular practice, not a one-time certification.

Belt placement matters. A medical pouch should be positioned on the support side, opposite the holster, to avoid interference with the draw stroke. Appendix carry pairs naturally with a support-side 9 o'clock medical pouch. The first 60 seconds of a trauma response are the critical window. An on-body IFAK, not a bag in the car, is the only configuration that meets that timeline.

Concealment training and basic medical training are the two most impactful skills a church security volunteer can develop. Firearm proficiency means little if the volunteer cannot stop bleeding in the aftermath.

Legal Compliance: Know Your State Before You Carry

Armed church volunteers operate under widely varying legal frameworks, and the landscape is shifting fast. What was legal in your state last year may not be legal today.

California's Senate Bill 1454, effective January 1, 2025, removed exemptions that previously allowed churches and nonprofits to operate volunteer security teams outside formal regulation. Armed roles in California now require a Private Patrol Operator (PPO) license.

Florida is moving in the opposite direction. Senate Bill 52, which passed the Florida Senate unanimously in February 2026, would authorize houses of worship to use armed volunteers without requiring a professional security license. This reflects a broader national legislative trend toward empowering church self-defense.

Volunteers must verify their state's current statute before carrying on church property. Laws are actively changing in 2025 and 2026. Church leadership should consult legal counsel and establish a written security policy that documents volunteer authorization, training requirements, and liability coverage. The best holster in the world does not protect a volunteer who is carrying without lawful authorization in their jurisdiction.

Build Your Church Security Loadout: A Practical Checklist
Carry position: Select AIWB or strong-side IWB based on body type, attire, and role. Train that position exclusively. Do not switch between indoor and outdoor phases.
Retention level: Level I passive Kydex for concealed volunteers. Level II if you patrol openly or may engage in physical confrontation.
Holster: Precision-molded Kydex with a defined retention click, low-profile clip, and optional claw/wing for concealment. Avoid soft holsters that collapse during reholstering.
Belt: Rigid gun belt rated for your firearm's weight, 1.5-inch minimum. A dress belt is not a gun belt.
Medical: Support-side IFAK with tourniquet, hemostatic gauze, and chest seal, carried on-body, not in a bag.
Training: Practice drawing from a seated position, from formal attire, and from a standing patrol posture. All three scenarios are realistic for a church security volunteer.
Legal: Verify your state's current statute on armed church volunteers before your first shift, and review it annually as legislation evolves. Consult legal counsel.
Faith and mission: Carry with the conviction of Romans 13:4. The role of protector within a congregation is a calling that demands the best gear, the best training, and the right mindset.

At C&G Holsters, our team of U.S. Military Veterans, LEOs, and competitive shooters builds every holster to the standard we carry ourselves. The calling to protect your congregation deserves gear that will not let you down when it matters most.

text:
Jordan Love's father wanted to name him Michael Jordan Love.

"That's real. Michael Jordan Love. My mom vetoed it, thank God."

His father was a sergeant for the Bakersfield Police Department. His mother was California Highway Patrol.

Here is the whole thing.

Orbin Love would work a double shift, pick his son up, and drive the police cruiser straight to the Little League field.

"He'd be in the outfield helping coach with his full BPD uniform on, beeper in the belt buckle and everything."

Everybody in town called him Big O.

There is a picture of Jordan as a baby that he still talks about. His dad had put him up on a racehorse.

"I'm like one, in my diaper, and I'm chilling up on some Secretariat-looking dude."

"He was literally always just there. To me, there's no higher praise for a dad."

His motto was two words.

Try everything.

"He just had this relentless positivity about him. In his mind, me and my sisters could really do anything."

Jordan was 14 when he lost him.

"My world was turned upside down. I wanted to quit football. Honestly, I kind of wanted to give up on everything."

His mother is named Anna. She asked him to give it one more year before he decided anything, and she told him this.

"If you keep playing football, you know I'll always be there for you."

He stayed.

He did not start for his high school varsity until the middle of his junior year. He came out a two star recruit, and Utah State was the only school in the top division of college football that offered him a scholarship.

Green Bay took him 26th. Then he sat three years behind Aaron Rodgers and did not play a snap his first season.

Here is what he wrote about that.

"I'm not Aaron Rodgers. I'm not a guy with a five-star pedigree."

He is the quarterback of the Packers now, on a 220 million dollar contract. Tonight he plays Dallas.

"I'm doing something that would've been beyond my father's wildest dreams."

And in May he became a father himself. Her name is Rayna Capri.

One more thing.

He runs a charity that buys new cleats every year for youth football teams. He named it Hands of 10ve, after his number.

He dedicated it to his dad.

Now the honest part. He has one playoff win in three seasons as the starter. Green Bay gave away a 21 to 6 fourth quarter lead and lost in January. A 220 million dollar contract buys a lot of patience, and it does not buy forever.

But the kid who wanted to quit everything is the one who stayed.

And the two words his father left him are the ones he is still doing it on.
