text:
Delta Air Lines waited seven years to bring back nonstop flights between New York JFK and Orange County. Now, just six months after their return, the airline is preparing to suspend them again.

Delta relaunched the route in May 2026, offering daily flights aboard Boeing 757-200s equipped with 16 lie-flat Delta One seats. The service gave passengers another premium option between New York and Southern California without having to travel through Los Angeles International Airport.

But according to Cirium schedule data cited by Simple Flying, Delta’s final flights are scheduled for November 29, with service expected to resume on May 6, 2027.

That leaves American Airlines as the only carrier operating nonstop between JFK and Orange County during Delta’s absence.

American has served the route since July 2021 and plans to continue flying daily. Its premium Airbus A321T aircraft offer 30 lie-flat seats, although the airline is gradually replacing that configuration as its new A321XLRs enter service.

United also connects Orange County with the New York area, but flies to Newark rather than JFK.

Delta hasn’t publicly explained the upcoming pause, so there’s no confirmed reason to suggest the route has underperformed.

Still, it’s an interesting reversal for a service that only returned in May. American spent years flying the route without Delta, briefly gained a competitor, and is now set to have JFK–Orange County to itself again until next spring.

text:
Paper: Same Inducement, Different Packaging — Cigarette Trades and Free-Food Ballot Events in California

Both the Skid Row cigarette-for-signature schemes and the Republican free-food ballot events rely on the same basic mechanism: a tangible benefit is used to move election documents. The difference is packaging. One version is a direct exchange that violates existing law and has been filmed and prosecuted. The other embeds the benefit inside a social event so that it remains legal under California’s current rules. Republicans running the food events are not inventing a new practice; they are adapting an existing incentive structure to the legal environment Democrats created and expanded.

 The Direct Version
On Skid Row, circulators offered cigarettes or a few dollars specifically in return for a signature on an initiative petition, and sometimes on a voter registration form. California Elections Code § 18603 makes it a misdemeanor to offer or give money or other valuable consideration in exchange for a petition signature. Undercover videos repeatedly captured these trades. Prosecutors treated the cigarettes as valuable consideration. The result was state charges in the 2016–2018 cycles with multiple guilty pleas, followed by later federal cases that involved the use of stolen voter identities. The transaction was simple and open: the item was conditioned on the signature. That is why enforcement followed.

 The Packaged Version
Republican groups, most visibly Carl DeMaio’s Reform California, host free food and drink events while people complete ballots, receive voter guides, and optionally leave their completed ballots for collection and delivery. Third-party ballot return is legal in California. The food is presented as hospitality at a political gathering rather than as payment for a signature or a vote. Under the 2025 statute (§ 18107.5), an offense requires either intent to induce voting or registration or a benefit that is contingent on the person actually voting or registering. Open free food without an explicit contingency has not produced the same enforcement. Earlier case law involving free tacos available to anyone, without conditioning them on voting, was not treated as illegal vote-buying. Organizers can therefore describe the events as ordinary turnout encouragement while still collecting ballots.

 Why the Packaging Works
DeMaio and similar Republicans state the strategy openly. Democrats legalized and used aggressive ballot collection after 2016–2018, and it contributed to Republican losses. Opposing the practice while refusing to use it is, in their view, self-defeating, so they match it under the existing rules and call their version “ballot harvesting done right.” The free food gets people to attend, stay, and hand over ballots without creating a recorded “pay for signature” exchange. Other California Republicans have promoted comparable “bring your own ballot” parties with food. From the perspective that treats both practices as the same underlying inducement, the cleverness consists of converting an activity that has been prosecuted when done directly into one that has not been prosecuted when staged as an event.

 Substance Versus Form
The practical effect in both settings is that more election paperwork moves because something of value was provided. In one case the benefit is small, immediate, and conditioned on the act, which violates § 18603. In the other the benefit is larger, social, and not formally conditioned, which has so far avoided liability under § 18107.5. The distinction is real under the statutes as written and enforced; whether it is meaningful depends on whether one focuses on the letter of the law or on the shared incentive structure. To date, the cigarette-for-signature exchanges have produced prosecutions. The free-food ballot events have not. That gap is the product of how the offer is structured, not the absence of an inducement.

text:
A POWERFUL ARTICLE BY SUSAN B. GLASSER IN THE NEW YORKER: IS TRUMP HELPING PUTIN WIN?

Trump’s Republican Party is barely holding on to both chambers of Congress, while his approval ratings are sinking to historic lows. Yet at this critical moment, the president has spent an entire week attacking Volodymyr Zelensky and openly helping Vladimir Putin in his war of aggression against Ukraine.

Zelensky is now publicly describing his conflict with Trump as an almost irreversible rupture. Ukraine is “losing a strong partner,” he told Piers Morgan. “It hurts when Trump chooses a side, and it isn't ours.” In an interview with the Financial Times, Zelensky also announced that Ukraine had observed Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire for three days but would no longer comply, despite American threats to suspend intelligence sharing. “That’s over,” he declared.

Timing is everything, both in war and in midterm elections. And this particular moment is extraordinarily dangerous. Trump’s special envoys are once again pressuring Kyiv to accept an agreement that looks far more like surrender than compromise.

“The moment of greatest danger is now,” warned Daniel Fried, a former senior American diplomat. Returning from meetings with security officials in Poland and Romania, Fried expressed deep concern not only about Ukraine’s position but also about Russia’s escalating attacks designed to test NATO allies. His greatest fear is that Putin recognizes this vulnerability and intends to exploit it immediately.

The question is whether anyone in Washington can—or even wants to—stop him, given Trump’s expansive interpretation of presidential authority and his apparent indifference to Congress.

Senator Chris Coons of Delaware offered an equally disturbing assessment. Trump’s worst instincts, he argued, continue to prevail: trusting Putin and treating the Russian dictator’s words as more important than the warnings of America’s allies.

Coons recalled the enormous effort required to persuade Trump to sign the Graham sanctions legislation against Russia. Now Trump has undermined his own Ukraine strategy, repeating a pattern that has become painfully familiar over the past decade. He takes a hesitant step toward helping Kyiv, speaks with Putin, and promptly returns to his instinctive preference for Moscow.

Can America repair its damaged relationship with European allies? Coons answered his own question: “Not while Trump is president.” He also warned that the damage Trump could inflict over the next two years is being seriously underestimated.

Even Republicans are increasingly alarmed. Six Republican senators recently condemned Trump’s Russian diesel agreement as a gift to an adversary and a betrayal of allies. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board called it a moral and strategic mistake, an assessment quickly amplified by Trump’s former vice president, Mike Pence.

Meanwhile, a new Fox News poll reportedly puts Trump’s approval rating at just 36%, with 70% of Americans disapproving of his handling of the economy.

Russia expert Angela Stent, who previously served as a senior intelligence analyst during the George W. Bush administration, suggests that Trump may be preparing Zelensky to become his political scapegoat. If Republicans suffer serious losses in November, Trump could blame Ukraine for high diesel prices and demand Zelensky’s departure.

But Americans struggling with their own economic problems are unlikely to embrace demands for Ukraine to remove its president. And Trump knows that Russian diesel, even if delivered, cannot arrive quickly enough to rescue Republicans before November 3.

This raises an even darker possibility, one that Susan B. Glasser leaves hanging over the entire discussion.

What if Trump is returning to Putin not because he believes it will help Republicans win the midterm elections, but because he genuinely wants Russia to win the war?

That is the question Americans—and the entire democratic world—must confront.
